newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-P&O half-year results beat forecasts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-P&O half-year results beat forecasts.

text.p: Shipping and construction group Peninsular & Oriental Steam Navigation Co announced better than expected half-year results on Tuesday but signalled a difficult second half as it gets to grips with its troubled container shipping and ferry businesses.

P&O said it made an underlying pre-tax profit of 130.2 million pounds ($202 million) on sales of 3.4 billion pounds for the six months to end-June, before adding a net gain of 4.5 million pounds on the sale of fixed assets.
Analysts forecasts had predicted pretax profits would drop back to 115-118 million pounds from last year's 131.9 million.
The firm also said it is to buy out Nedlloyd NV's share in North Sea Ferries for 25.25 million pounds, the second deal between P&O and the Dutch group this month.
Nedlloyd and P&O announced last week they intend to merge their container shipping businesses into a $1.5 billion giant because of increasing global competition.
"Having announced an important step forward for containers we are now focusing on rationalising the ferry business," P&0 chairman Lord Sterling said on Tuesday.
Sterling warned of a difficult second half for both the containers and ferry businesses but the company has now set a new course for the longer term.
But P&O's share price dipped four pence to 590-1/2p after the results on lack of any more real news since the company delighted the market with its container deal last week.

Sterling said the North Sea Ferries (NSF) deal was the first move in what was expected to be a major rationalisation of ferry operators battling furiously in the English Channel for market share against the new Eurotunnel railway.

But P&O already owns 50 percent of North Sea Ferries and said NSF has not been hit by the war with Eurotunnel on the high volume routes to the south, leaving it to make "better profits through increased volumes and reasonable rates."
Buying out Nedlloyd would allow P&O to absorb NSF into its own operations and save some five million pounds in costs a year, Sterling said.
In contrast, total traffic in the key Dover-Calais market was up 15 percent on a year ago but P&O had seen its own traffic fall "and we continue to make losses," he said.

Consequently he said P&O was now talking to rivals about rationalisation following Britain's decision now that Eurotunnel is established to lift its ban on any sort of collaboration between the big ferry operators P&O and Stena Line.
"We have now started talks," Sterling said.

In the six months P&O Ferries made an overall operating profit of just 500,000 pounds, down from 24.8 million in the same period a year ago when Eurotunnel was still building up its market share to the near 50 percent now claimed.

"In terms of (traffic) volume the second half should not see such a significant relative reduction year on year since Eurotunnel was moving towards full operation in the second half of 1995," Sterling said.
P&O Ferries carried 11 percent fewer cross-Channel passenger vehicles than in second quarter 1995, an improvement on its first quarter deficit of 23 percent.

Looking at the rest of the group, Sterling said its cruise liners division is expected to have a good second half, having made an operating profit of 67.5 million pounds in the first half, up from 48.2 million pounds a year ago.
He said the business services, exhibition, housebuilding and construction divisions "are also expected to do well."

Container shipping's operating profits rose to 20.9 million pounds from 15.3 million last time but Sterling warned that "conditions are becoming increasingly competitive, particularly on the main Far East to Europe trade."

Sterling also warned on the hard-pressed bulk shipping business, where operating profits fell to 2.6 million pounds from 10.3 million pounds last time, that the company "does not foresee any improvement in rates from dry bulk shipping for the remained of this year."
